notes: Level 5 with a multi-site diagnostic accuracy design, a late reply refused after an investigator edit, and dependency closure between Protocol and Stats. Seven fixture records are appraised; one annotation gives relevance 105, stored null with issue out-of-range (never clamped). The supported decision is accepted with both gates met. After Protocol and Stats are complete for three clinics, the investigator starts Ethics; while that request is pending, the investigator records on screen that clinic C has paused (set-field protocol.population), which flags Stats for review (G8). The held reply is encoded as illuminate (request sent, reply held), set-field, then wait (reply delivered), because the format has no field for a held reply. The studyRevision guard itself is in the 875fe59 library (store.ts mergeStageIfRevision); applying it on the screen is L1.2 wiring, not a work-order entry. inputs.need:
I lead digital health for a primary care organisation with three clinics (A, B and C) and about 38,000 patients. Since we opened the patient portal to everyone in 2023, secure messages to clinicians have risen by about 70 percent, and our physicians and nurse practitioners now spend a median of 1.4 hours a day on portal messages, much of it after clinic hours. Some messages are urgent, such as new chest pain, a child with a high fever or a medication reaction, and they wait for hours in the same queue as prescription requests and appointment questions.

Our electronic record vendor offers an automated triage flag that reads each incoming message and marks it as needing same-day clinical attention or not. Before we switch it on, we want a diagnostic accuracy study across the three clinics: run the flag silently on incoming messages for a few months and compare it with a reference standard of two clinicians independently reviewing each sampled message without seeing the flag. The clinics differ: clinic B serves many older patients, and clinic C has many patients who write in languages other than English.

I need help with sampling the messages, how many we need to estimate sensitivity for urgent messages with useful precision, how to build the reference standard and handle disagreement, what to report besides accuracy (for example how much clinician time might be saved and which urgent messages would be missed), and how to handle privacy when clinicians read message text for this purpose. We have a small quality budget, an informatics nurse, and clinicians willing to review messages for two hours a week.
inputs.constraints: Quality budget of 12,000. Informatics nurse 1 day per week and reviewing clinicians 2 hours per week each until June 2027. The triage flag may run only in silent mode; no clinical action on its output during the study.

records.title: Accuracy of a natural language processing triage flag for urgent patient portal messages: a validation study in primary care
records.authors: Nakamura-Obi E, Fairbairn-Adeyemi T, Castellano-Hurst M
records.abstract: We ran an automated triage flag on 2,400 randomly sampled portal messages from four primary care practices and compared it with a reference standard of two clinicians reviewing each message independently, with a third resolving disagreements. Urgent messages made up 4 percent of the sample. Sensitivity for urgent messages was 86 percent (95 percent CI 79 to 91) and specificity was 91 percent. Sensitivity was 71 percent for messages written in languages other than English. Most missed urgent messages combined several requests, with the urgent one last. The authors caution that accuracy may differ in other patient populations.

records.title: Patient portal message volume and physicians' after-hours work: a multi-site analysis
records.abstract: We linked electronic record audit logs for 212 primary care physicians to their daily portal message counts over one year. Each additional 10 messages per day was associated with 23 minutes more work in the record outside scheduled hours. Physicians in the highest fifth of message volume reported higher burnout scores. Messages about medications and test results took longest to handle. The analysis could not separate message volume from other features of busy practices, and it did not record who wrote the messages or how urgent they were.

records.title: Reference standards for patient message triage studies: agreement between clinicians
records.abstract: Two clinicians independently rated the urgency of 900 patient portal messages without clinical context beyond the message and the problem list. Agreement on whether a message needed same-day attention was moderate (kappa 0.62). A third clinician adjudicated disagreements, which involved 14 percent of messages. Disagreement was most common for messages describing chronic symptoms that had changed, and for messages from carers. The authors recommend a written urgency definition with examples, calibration before rating, and adjudication rather than consensus discussion, and they report that rating took about one minute per message.

records.title: Automated triage of patient messages: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy
records.authors: Petersen-Achebe K, Morrow-Tanaka S, Diallo-Whitfield C
records.abstract: We included 12 studies of automated triage of patient messages. Reported sensitivity for urgent messages ranged from 62 to 94 percent. Most studies were at high risk of bias in the reference standard, because a single clinician rated messages or raters knew the automated result. Spectrum bias was common: several studies enriched samples with obviously urgent messages. Only 2 studies were multi-site, and none reported accuracy by patient language or age. The review recommends independent double rating and random sampling.

records.title: Clinicians' experience of managing patient portal messages: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 24 physicians and nurse practitioners about portal messages. Participants described answering messages in the evening, guilt about delays, and fear of missing an urgent message among routine requests. Several were cautious about automated triage and wanted to know how often it would miss urgent messages before relying on it. Participants suggested that a flag should route urgent messages to a clinician quickly rather than decide what could wait. Nurse practitioners described triaging messages for physicians without protected time, and several participants had changed their working hours to keep up with the queue.

records.title: Language, age and the content of patient portal messages in primary care
records.abstract: We described 5,000 portal messages from three clinics. Messages from patients aged over 75 more often contained several requests in one message. Messages written in languages other than English were three times as likely to be routed to the wrong staff member by reception teams. Carers wrote a fifth of messages for patients over 80. The report recommends that any automated routing be tested separately for older patients, carers and messages in languages other than English. It did not assess clinical urgency or outcomes.

records.title: Spectrum effects in the accuracy of message triage across clinic populations
records.abstract: We validated the same message triage flag in five clinics with different patient populations against a two-clinician reference standard. Sensitivity for urgent messages varied from 74 to 90 percent across clinics, and was lowest in the clinic with the most messages in languages other than English. Specificity varied less. Pooling clinics hid these differences. The authors recommend reporting accuracy by clinic and by message language, and sampling enough urgent messages in each clinic to do so. The reference standard was the same in every clinic.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A validation study and a five-clinic study report sensitivity for urgent messages in the 74 to 90 percent range, lower for messages in languages other than English, and a review of 12 studies finds reference standards at high risk of bias and few multi-site studies. Clinician agreement on urgency is only moderate without adjudication. Message volume is linked to after-hours work, and clinicians want the miss rate before relying on a flag. A multi-site study with an adjudicated reference standard, random sampling and results by clinic and language is needed.
response.gradeRationale: Few accuracy studies, variable by population, with frequent reference standard bias; workload evidence observational.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims; certainty low. One annotation carried an out-of-range relevance.
